title: Acts 23:12–35
context: More than forty men vow not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul, planning an ambush with the chief priests’ help. Paul’s nephew hears of the plot and reports it to Paul and then to the commander. The commander sends Paul by night under heavy guard to Governor Felix in Caesarea, with a letter explaining that Paul is accused only over questions of Jewish law and has done nothing deserving death or chains. Felix agrees to hear the case when the accusers arrive and keeps Paul in Herod’s palace.

verses.text: When it was day, some of the Jews banded together and bound themselves under a curse, saying that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.
verses.arminianNotes: At daybreak some Jews band together and bind themselves under a curse not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul.
verses.reformedNotes: The oath is a self-curse invoking God against themselves if they fail. Their religious intensity is aimed at murder.

verses.text: There were more than forty people who had made this conspiracy.
verses.arminianNotes: More than forty men join the conspiracy, a serious threat for a man in custody.
verses.reformedNotes: The size of the plot sets up how God will overturn it through a single young man.

verses.text: They came to the chief priests and the elders, and said, “We have bound ourselves under a great curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.
verses.arminianNotes: They inform the chief priests and elders of their vow, seeking help. Religious leaders are drawn into a murder plot.
verses.reformedNotes: The leaders’ willingness to cooperate exposes how far the hostility has gone.

verses.text: Now therefore, you with the council inform the commanding officer that he should bring him down to you tomorrow, as though you were going to judge his case more exactly. We are ready to kill him before he comes near.”
verses.arminianNotes: The council is to ask the commander to bring Paul down again on a pretext of further inquiry, and the assassins will kill him on the way.
verses.reformedNotes: The plan depends on deceiving the Roman officer, the same one who rescued Paul twice.

verses.text: But Paul’s sister’s son heard they were lying in wait, and he came and entered into the barracks and told Paul.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul’s nephew, his sister’s son, hears of the ambush and enters the barracks to tell him. This is the only glimpse of Paul’s family in the New Testament.
verses.reformedNotes: God’s protection comes through an unnamed relative who happens to hear. The promise of verse 11 is kept by very ordinary means.

verses.text: Paul summoned one of the centurions and said, “Bring this young man to the commanding officer, for he has something to tell him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Paul calls a centurion and asks him to take the young man to the commander. Paul trusts God’s promise and still acts sensibly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed writers point to this as an example of providence working through human prudence rather than replacing it.

verses.text: So he took him and brought him to the commanding officer and said, “Paul, the prisoner, summoned me and asked me to bring this young man to you. He has something to tell you.”
verses.arminianNotes: The centurion brings him, explaining that the prisoner Paul asked for this.
verses.reformedNotes: Paul’s good standing with his guards makes the message travel quickly.

verses.text: The commanding officer took him by the hand, and going aside, asked him privately, “What is it that you have to tell me?”
verses.arminianNotes: The commander takes the young man by the hand and leads him aside privately, a touch of kindness from a senior officer.
verses.reformedNotes: The commander’s care for confidentiality allows the plan to be thwarted without tipping off the conspirators.

verses.text: He said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though intending to inquire somewhat more accurately concerning him.
verses.arminianNotes: The nephew relays the plot: the council will ask for Paul tomorrow as if to inquire more closely.
verses.reformedNotes: His account matches verses 14–15 exactly, giving the commander reason to believe him.

verses.text: Therefore don’t yield to them, for more than forty men lie in wait for him, who have bound themselves under a curse to neither eat nor drink until they have killed him. Now they are ready, looking for the promise from you.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Don’t yield to them,” he urges; more than forty men are waiting and have sworn an oath. A young man speaks boldly to a Roman tribune.
verses.reformedNotes: The detail that they are “now ready” adds urgency. The commander must act that night.

verses.text: So the commanding officer let the young man go, charging him, “Tell no one that you have revealed these things to me.”
verses.arminianNotes: The commander dismisses him with orders to tell no one.
verses.reformedNotes: Secrecy protects both the young man and the plan to move Paul.

verses.text: He called to himself two of the centurions, and said, “Prepare two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, with seventy horsemen and two hundred men armed with spears, at the third hour of the night.”
verses.arminianNotes: He orders two centurions to prepare two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen to leave at nine that night for Caesarea.
verses.reformedNotes: Nearly five hundred troops escort one prisoner. The scale reflects both the danger and the commander’s concern to avoid blame.

verses.text: He asked them to provide mounts, that they might set Paul on one, and bring him safely to Felix the governor.
verses.arminianNotes: Mounts are provided so Paul can be brought safely to Felix the governor.
verses.reformedNotes: Felix, a former slave who rose to govern Judea, was known to Tacitus for cruelty and lust. Paul is heading into another uncertain court.

verses.text: He wrote a letter like this:
verses.arminianNotes: The commander writes a letter, which Luke reproduces in summary form.
verses.reformedNotes: The letter is the first official Roman document about Paul’s case in Acts.

verses.text: “Claudius Lysias to the most excellent governor Felix: Greetings.
verses.arminianNotes: “Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent governor Felix: greetings.” This is the first time the commander’s name appears.
verses.reformedNotes: The formal greeting follows the standard pattern of Greek letters of the period.

verses.text: “This man was seized by the Jews, and was about to be killed by them when I came with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman.
verses.arminianNotes: Lysias claims he rescued Paul after learning he was a Roman, quietly reversing the order of events and omitting the near-scourging.
verses.reformedNotes: The letter is a small study in self-interest: the official edits the record to look good.

verses.text: Desiring to know the cause why they accused him, I brought him down to their council.
verses.arminianNotes: He says he brought Paul before the council to learn the charge.
verses.reformedNotes: This part of the report is accurate and shows Lysias trying to follow procedure.

verses.text: I found him to be accused about questions of their law, but not to be charged with anything worthy of death or of imprisonment.
verses.arminianNotes: He found Paul accused about questions of Jewish law, with nothing deserving death or chains. This is the first Roman declaration of Paul’s innocence.
verses.reformedNotes: Luke records several such verdicts (25:25; 26:31). Like Jesus, Paul is repeatedly found innocent by those who hold him.

verses.text: When I was told that the Jews lay in wait for the man, I sent him to you immediately, charging his accusers also to bring their accusations against him before you. Farewell.”
verses.arminianNotes: Informed of a plot, he sent Paul at once and told the accusers to state their case before Felix.
verses.reformedNotes: Transferring the case removes it from Jerusalem’s pressure and places it in Roman hands.

verses.text: So the soldiers, carrying out their orders, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris.
verses.arminianNotes: The soldiers take Paul by night as far as Antipatris, about forty miles, through hill country where ambush was likely.
verses.reformedNotes: Luke records the route precisely, as if from someone who knew the road.

verses.text: But on the next day they left the horsemen to go with him, and returned to the barracks.
verses.arminianNotes: Once the danger zone is past, the foot soldiers return and the cavalry continue with Paul.
verses.reformedNotes: The escort is scaled down once the threat recedes, a sensible military detail.

verses.text: When they came to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they also presented Paul to him.
verses.arminianNotes: At Caesarea they deliver the letter and present Paul to the governor.
verses.reformedNotes: Caesarea, Rome’s administrative capital in Judea, becomes Paul’s home for the next two years.

verses.text: When the governor had read it, he asked what province he was from. When he understood that he was from Cilicia, he said,
verses.arminianNotes: Felix reads the letter and asks Paul’s province; learning it is Cilicia, he accepts jurisdiction.
verses.reformedNotes: Cilicia was then administered with Syria, so Felix could hear the case without sending Paul home.

verses.text: “I will hear you fully when your accusers also arrive.” He commanded that he be kept in Herod’s palace.
verses.arminianNotes: He promises a full hearing when the accusers arrive and orders Paul kept in Herod’s praetorium, the palace built by Herod the Great.
verses.reformedNotes: Paul is confined in a former royal palace, safe from ambush, while God’s promise about Rome waits for its time.
